transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-14 15:30 PT / 42m
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Lina (Redwood SE), Jared (Redwood Solutions), Markus, Gita, Hannah, Leo (NimbleRx)

Summary: Quick POC check-in focused on throughput tuning. Reviewed last week's soak test, discussed continuous batching behavior at low-latency targets, agreed a queue-gating approach + concurrency caps for production ramp, and set next steps for a 4-hour burst soak and line-item telemetry to compare tail latencies.

Topics: results review; continuous batching anomalies; gate thresholds; concurrency target; backpressure & retries; telemetry to capture (per-token latency, batch sizes, queue depth); next steps and owners.

[00:00] Samir: okay hi everyone thanks for joining, we'll try to keep this tight. we ran the batch soak from last week, lina can you start with the quick highlights?

[00:22] Lina: yeah uh quick highlights. so baseline: staging workload mirrored 60% of production qps with a 95th token latency target of 350ms. we saw average batch size drift between 1.6 and 2.8 depending on ramp segments, and KV cache hits were stable at ~72%. the oddity was during burst windows we saw a sudden p99 token spike up to ~1.8s which correlated with queue depth hitting the manual threshold. afaict there was some queue-gating thrash when concurrency jumped.

[01:10] Markus: yep that's what we saw. during the 30s bursts our autoscale didn't kick fast enough and the requests stacked, then the queue gate opened and closed a few times. seemed like a feedback loop.

[01:28] Gita: quick question — when you say 'queue gate' can you, uh, describe the behavior? is it rejecting or just delaying at the proxy?

[01:36] Lina: good callout. currently the staging gate delays at the router layer, it holds requests in a soft queue and applies a backpressure signal to the caller after X ms. we saw the soft queue flush into the runtime and produce a lot of small batches which hurt throughput and raised tail latency.

[02:05] Leo: and that was during the lane shift where we changed from a 150ms to 80ms gating timer? I recall we reduced the threshold to be more aggressive.

[02:15] Lina: exactly. tradeoff: tighter gate reduces in-flight concurrency and gives lower average latency for stable loads but if the burst amplitude is high you get more single-request batches.

[02:36] Samir: okay so the playbook we're proposing: adaptive queue-gating with hysteresis + concurrency caps per node, plus a short burst window that allows temporary burst capacity (burst tokens) without immediately opening the gate. that way we avoid thrash.

[02:58] Hannah: can you unpack hysteresis? like concrete numbers for us to try?

[03:05] Lina: sure. example numbers: open gate when queue depth > 80 for 3s, close gate when queue depth < 40 for 6s. concurrency cap per GPU worker set to 6 active requests (we tuned from 4 up to 6), and a 60s burst allowance where we can exceed cap by up to 25% before we start shedding. the parameters are tunable of course.

[03:40] Markus: that seems reasonable. our concern is p99 spikes — is there a way to correlate spikes to batch composition? we need artifact-level telemetry.

[03:51] Lina: yes we recommend instrumenting per-batch histograms: batch size, formation latency, kernel exec time, kvcache hit boolean, and which model variant was used. that lets us attribute tail to either tiny-batch overhead or a slow kernel selection.

[04:14] Gita: on the model side we're using a quantized 7B variant with some custom LoRA. does that change recommendations around concurrency?

[04:25] Lina: slightly — quantized runs tend to have more variable kernel latencies depending on sequence length. we bumped concurrency to 6 because it improved aggregate throughput in our bench but you should run a short sweep. we can provide a script to iterate concurrency 4,6,8 and capture tokens/sec and p99.

[04:49] Samir: important note: continuous batching logic in the runtime prefers waiting for more requests up to a soft timeout; if that timeout is too long you'll see good throughput but higher median latency. shorter timeout pushes small batches and harms throughput. the playbook's hysteresis + burst window aims to keep that timeout tuned dynamically.

[05:12] Leo: does Redwood's runtime expose the batching timeout metric? where do we read that?

[05:18] Lina: yes, it's exported as batch_wait_ms and batch_size_avg per worker via prometheus. we'll add suggested grafana panels to the playbook.

[05:29] Jared: also note the KV cache eviction metric — we saw 'KV cash' in one of the transcripts — but the real thing is kv_cache_hit_rate which when below ~60% tends to push up token op time.

[05:42] Gita: got it. the other question: what about retry semantics? we had some retries at the client that probably increased load and confused the gate.

[05:50] Lina: you should move to an idempotent-aware retry policy and exponential backoff with jitter; moreover prefer immediate 429s for queued rejects so callers back off quickly instead of retrying aggressively.

[06:07] Hannah: regulatory ques — when you talk about shedding or rejecting into the gate, will that surface in audit logs? we need to track dropped vs delayed for compliance.

[06:16] Samir: yes, all gateway actions are logged and available in the console, including reason codes: delay, shed, fallback. we can also stream to your SIEM or S3 bucket.

[06:28] Markus: okay next — we ran a short soak with concurrency 6 and gate timers per Lina's earlier doc, results attached in the deck. summary: throughput improved ~14% over previous run, p95 stayed under 420ms, but p99 still had intermittent spikes.

[06:45] Lina: those spikes lined up with two specific patterns: 1) sudden drop in batch size to 1 or 2 during ramp down, 2) one outlier worker had a slow kernel path at seqlen=1024. we saw node-level wide variance.

[07:05] Leo: how do we handle node-level variance? Is the recommended solution to pin model variants or to isolate noisy hosts?

[07:12] Lina: two options: isolate noisy hosts via node label + taint in k8s so they only serve less critical traffic, or apply per-host health checks to auto-outscore. for pilot we recommend isolating the outlier nodes and letting us profile the kernel path.

[07:31] Gita: can Redwood run a remote profiler on the node? we can open a support tunnel.

[07:36] Samir: yes we can. we'll need your permission for temporary access — we use a read-only profiling agent and we provide the exact minimal commands in the security packet.

[07:46] Hannah: security packet — we need SOC2 attestation and KMS integration details before any support tunnel.

[07:52] Samir: noted. we'll attach SOC2 and KMS docs in the follow-up, plus the exact scope for the tunnel.

[07:58] Markus: cool. next point — capacity planning. our SREs want a clear concurrency ladder for ramp: start at 60% qps with concurrency 4, after 24h move to concurrency 6 and 90% qps, then allow burst window enabling up to 125% for 1h. is that approach okay?

[08:22] Lina: that's a sensible ladder. we recommend gating at the route layer and adding a model-variant fallback to a cheaper, lower-latency model if we detect sustained queue > threshold for > 10m. that provides graceful degradation.

[08:36] Leo: fallback concerns — will fallback change output shape? we have downstream consumers.

[08:42] Lina: it can, so you should use a compatibility-aware fallback or add an explicit header so your downstream can accept different variant. we'll document that.

[08:52] Hannah: any billing implications for burst capacity in dedicated pool?

[08:57] Samir: for Dedicated we can set a burst credit pool, it's accounted separately as a burst surcharge. we'll send a numeric example in the pricing follow-up.

[09:08] Markus: good. can we talk about telemetry aggregation? what logs and traces do we need to make decisions after the soak?

[09:16] Lina: minimal telemetry set: per-request trace id, batch formation time, batch size, worker id, batch exec time, kvcache hit boolean, model variant, node kernel path label. aggregate panels: batch_size histograms, queue_depth timeseries, token_throughput, p50/p95/p99 token latency by route.

[09:39] Gita: we'll add those to our observability checklist. who owns creating the grafana dashboard?

[09:44] Samir: Lina will provide a starter dashboard json and recommended alerts. Jared can assist with alert threshold suggestions.

[09:52] Lina: I'll attach the dashboard and the helm snippet for queue gating.

[09:58] Hannah: last item — we want one more short experiment: disable per-request jitter in the client for a 2-hour window to see if jitter interacts badly with gate timers. is that worth doing?

[10:10] Lina: yes, disable jitter for that window, run the soak, capture batch-size distribution. if we see worse tails, revert.

[10:20] Markus: ok let's outline the next steps then.

Recap: 1) Redwood to run 4-hour soak with adaptive gate + burst window and share logs. 2) NimbleRx to supply two prod traces and traffic curve. 3) Samir/Lina to share playbook, helm values, grafana dashboard, SOC2/KMS docs, and profiler access steps. 4) Follow-up hands-on tuning session 10/21.

Outro: thanks everyone, we'll circulate notes and links to the deck and the playbook in the next email.
